lesson_title: Not Robbing Your Own Team: Corporate Governance and Ethics
hook_text: The treasurer bought the team's kit from her sister's shop. The price was fair. It was still a scandal — here's why.
clip_script: Sondela Netball Club has a hundred and fifty members. Each paid a joining fee, and that money bought the posts, the dresses, the storeroom. The members OWN the club — but a hundred and fifty people cannot run one club, so once a year they elect a committee of seven to run it for them. The members keep the votes, the yearly report-back, and the right to ask the treasurer exactly where June's gate money went. The committee gets the fixtures, the kit orders, the bank card. And the treasurer's rand is not the treasurer's — every cent belongs to the people who trusted her with it. Companies write that deal into law and call it fiduciary duty. Now the scandal. The treasurer, Zanele, orders the new match dresses from her sister's shop — no other quotes, decided alone. Even if the price was fair, the decision was never protected: she had a personal interest and never declared it. The repair: declare the family connection, step out of the decision, let the committee gather three quotes, minute the choice. Same conflict, handled cleanly — and her sister's shop may still win, honestly this time. That is corporate governance: problem, principle, remedy. A company is just this club, with more zeros on the statement.
visual_style: A netball clubhouse with a wall of member photos; a ballot box electing seven silhouettes; a bank card passing from many small figures to one; the kit order splitting into a shadowed private path versus a bright three-quote path with minutes being written.
pacing: Warm scene-setting, a tension spike at the sister's shop, methodical beat-by-beat repair, clean landing on problem-principle-remedy.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn the three-move method that answers every governance scenario.
